stimuli.title: Enzyme investigation
stimuli.text:
Catalase is an enzyme in liver cells that breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen gas. A student placed equal pieces of fresh liver into equal volumes of hydrogen peroxide at different temperatures and measured the oxygen produced in 2 minutes.

| Temperature (C) | Oxygen produced (mL) |
|---|---|
| 10 | 6 |
| 20 | 11 |
| 30 | 17 |
| 40 | 19 |
| 50 | 8 |
| 60 | 1 |

stimuli.title: A short gene and three mutations
stimuli.text:
The mRNA made from a short gene is shown below, split into codons. A scientist found three mutant versions of the gene and wrote out the mRNA each one makes.

| Version | mRNA |
|---|---|
| Normal | AUG GAA CCA UUU GGC UAA |
| Mutant 1 | AUG GUA CCA UUU GGC UAA |
| Mutant 2 | AUG GAA UCC AUU UGG CUA A |
| Mutant 3 | AUG GAG CCA UUU GGC UAA |

Part of the genetic code: AUG = methionine (start), GAA = glutamic acid, GAG = glutamic acid, GUA = valine, CCA = proline, UUU = phenylalanine, GGC = glycine, UAA = stop.

stimuli.title: Flower color cross
stimuli.text:
In a garden plant, the allele for red flowers (R) and the allele for white flowers (W) show incomplete dominance: RR plants have red flowers, RW plants have pink flowers and WW plants have white flowers. A student crossed two pink-flowered plants and grew 200 of their seeds.

| Flower color | Number of offspring |
|---|---|
| Red | 52 |
| Pink | 97 |
| White | 51 |

stimuli.title: Beetles on dark soil
stimuli.text:
A population of beetles lives on light brown soil. Beetle color is inherited, and birds eat the beetles they can see easily. A fire darkened the soil. A scientist counted beetles of each color in the same area every two years.

| Year | Light beetles | Dark beetles |
|---|---|---|
| 0 (fire) | 450 | 50 |
| 2 | 310 | 90 |
| 4 | 180 | 170 |
| 6 | 70 | 260 |

Each beetle lays many more eggs than can survive to adulthood.

stimuli.title: A grassland food chain
stimuli.text:
A student modeled the energy in one grassland food chain. The numbers show the energy stored in each trophic level each year.

| Organism | Trophic level | Energy (kilocalories per square meter) |
|---|---|---|
| Grasses | Producer | 20,000 |
| Grasshoppers | Primary consumer | 2,000 |
| Mice | Secondary consumer | 200 |
| Hawks | Tertiary consumer | ? |

stimuli.title: Wolves and elk
stimuli.text:
Wolves were returned to a large park where elk had grazed with no wolves for many years. Scientists recorded the elk population and the number of young willow trees growing along streams.

| Year | Wolves | Elk | Young willows per 100 m of stream |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 16,000 | 4 |
| 5 | 40 | 12,000 | 9 |
| 10 | 90 | 8,000 | 21 |
| 15 | 100 | 7,000 | 30 |

questions.stem: Which biomolecule makes up most of the cell membrane and forms a barrier that water-soluble substances cannot easily cross?
questions.explanation: A membrane is a bilayer of phospholipids whose fatty acid tails are nonpolar, so ions and other water-soluble substances do not pass through easily. Starch is a storage carbohydrate, not a membrane material.

questions.stem: A scientist finds a single-celled organism with ribosomes, a cell membrane and a cell wall, but no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. The organism is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Lacking a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles is what defines a prokaryote such as a bacterium. Plants, fungi and protists are eukaryotes, which all have a nucleus, even though some of them also have cell walls.

questions.stem: Which two observations support the idea that mitochondria were once free-living prokaryotes? Choose two.
options: They divide by splitting in two
They have their own circular DNA
They use oxygen to release energy
They are found in animal cells
They are smaller than the nucleus
questions.explanation: Endosymbiotic theory points to features mitochondria share with bacteria: their own circular DNA and division by splitting, separate from the cell cycle. Using oxygen or being found in animal cells does not link them to prokaryotes.

questions.stem: Why are antibiotics not used to treat the common cold, which is caused by a virus?
options: Viruses lack the cell parts antibiotics target
Viruses have cell walls that block antibiotics
Viruses only infect cells of plants
Viruses are too large for antibiotics to enter
questions.explanation: Antibiotics act on structures and processes of bacterial cells, such as cell walls and bacterial ribosomes. A virus is a protein coat around genetic material with no cell parts of its own, so there is nothing for an antibiotic to act on.

questions.skill: B.6A Cell cycle and DNA replication
questions.stem: During which stage of the cell cycle is DNA copied?
questions.explanation: The cell replicates its DNA during the S (synthesis) phase of interphase, before mitosis begins. In anaphase the copies are already made and are pulled apart.

questions.stem: Nerve cells and skin cells in one person contain the same DNA, yet they look and work very differently. This is because:
options: nerve cells lost most of their genes
skin cells copy their DNA incorrectly
each cell type has different DNA
questions.explanation: Cell differentiation happens when cells switch on different sets of genes, so they make different proteins. The DNA itself is the same in almost every body cell.

questions.skill: B.6C Cell cycle disruptions and cancer
questions.stem: A mutation stops a protein that normally halts the cell cycle when DNA is damaged. Which outcome is most likely?
options: The cell becomes a stem cell
questions.explanation: Checkpoint proteins pause the cycle so damage can be repaired or the cell can die. Without that brake, cells with damaged DNA divide and pass errors on, which can lead to a tumor.

questions.stem: At which temperature did catalase work fastest in this investigation?
questions.explanation: The most oxygen, 19 mL, was produced at 40 C, so the reaction ran fastest there. Production fell sharply at 50 C and 60 C.

questions.stem: Which explanation best accounts for the result at 60 C?
options: The peroxide became a new enzyme
questions.explanation: Too much heat denatures the enzyme, changing the shape of its active site so hydrogen peroxide no longer fits. Slow-moving molecules explain the low rate at 10 C, not at 60 C.

questions.stem: How did catalase affect the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide?
options: It added heat energy to the reaction
It was used up in the reaction
questions.explanation: Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy. They are not used up, so the same enzyme molecule can act again and again.

questions.stem: After a meal, nutrients absorbed in the small intestine reach the body's cells. Which two systems work together most directly to do this?
questions.explanation: The digestive system breaks food down and absorbs nutrients through the intestine wall, and the circulatory system carries those nutrients in the blood to every cell.

questions.stem: When blood glucose rises, the pancreas releases insulin, and cells take up more glucose. This interaction between the endocrine system and body cells is an example of:
options: absorption of water by the skin
questions.explanation: Insulin lowers blood glucose back toward its normal level, a feedback loop that maintains homeostasis. Regulation is one of the functions animal systems share.

questions.stem: Water absorbed by the roots of a tall tree reaches the leaves through:
questions.explanation: Xylem is the vascular tissue that carries water and minerals up from the roots. Phloem carries sugars made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

questions.stem: Each nucleotide in a DNA molecule is made of a phosphate group, a nitrogen base and:
questions.explanation: DNA nucleotides contain the sugar deoxyribose, which gives deoxyribonucleic acid its name. Ribose is the sugar in RNA.

questions.stem: One strand of DNA has the base sequence ATG CCA. What is the sequence of the matching strand?
questions.explanation: In DNA, A pairs with T and C pairs with G, so ATG CCA pairs with TAC GGT. U appears only in RNA.

questions.skill: B.7B Gene expression and protein synthesis
questions.stem: During transcription, the information in a gene is copied into:
questions.explanation: In transcription, RNA polymerase reads one strand of a gene and builds a matching mRNA molecule. Ribosomes later translate that mRNA into a protein.

questions.stem: A substitution changes one base in a gene, but the protein made from the gene is unchanged. Which explanation is most likely?
options: The cell stopped making the protein
Both codons code for one amino acid
The base was replaced in an RNA molecule
questions.explanation: Most amino acids have more than one codon, so some substitutions are silent. Other substitutions do change an amino acid or create a stop codon.

questions.stem: Which ratio of red to pink to white offspring does a Punnett square predict for this cross?
questions.explanation: RW x RW gives 1/4 RR, 1/2 RW and 1/4 WW, a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio of red to pink to white. The student's 52 : 97 : 51 is close to that.

questions.stem: Why do these results show incomplete dominance rather than complete dominance?
options: Only white plants survive the cross
The red allele hides the white allele
Both colors appear as patches on one flower
questions.explanation: With complete dominance, RW plants would look like one parent. Here they are pink, in between red and white. Patches of both colors on one flower would be codominance.

questions.stem: The student crosses a pink plant with a white plant. What percent of the offspring are expected to be pink?
questions.explanation: RW x WW gives RW and WW in equal numbers, so half the offspring are pink and half are white. No red offspring are possible.

questions.stem: The pink parent plants each made gametes by meiosis. Each gamete carried:
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so each gamete gets one chromosome of each pair and one allele of each gene. Fertilization restores two alleles.

questions.stem: The forelimbs of a human, a bat and a whale have the same arrangement of bones but are used for different tasks. These structures are evidence of common ancestry because they are:
questions.explanation: Homologous structures share an underlying pattern inherited from a common ancestor, even when their uses differ. Analogous structures, such as bird and insect wings, do similar jobs but have different origins.

questions.stem: The amino acid sequence of a protein is compared across species. Which result suggests two species share the most recent common ancestor?
options: They live in the same habitat
questions.explanation: Differences in DNA and protein sequences build up over time after species split, so species with the fewest differences most likely shared an ancestor more recently.

questions.skill: B.9B Rates of change in the fossil record
questions.stem: Fossils of a group of marine animals show almost no change in body form over millions of years, then several new forms appear in a short span of rock layers. Which two patterns does this record show?
questions.explanation: Long periods with little change are called stasis, and new forms showing up quickly in the record are called abrupt appearance. Gradualism would show slow, steady change through many layers.

questions.skill: B.10A Natural selection acts on populations
questions.stem: A student says, "A rabbit grew thicker fur during a cold winter, so its babies will have thicker fur." Why is this not an example of natural selection?
options: Rabbits cannot grow thicker fur in winter
Traits gained in life are not inherited
Cold weather changes the rabbit's DNA
questions.explanation: Natural selection changes the frequency of inherited traits in a population over generations. A trait an individual develops during its life is not passed on in its genes.

questions.stem: Which condition is necessary for natural selection to change a population?
options: Every individual has the same traits
questions.explanation: Selection needs inherited variation to act on. If every individual were the same, or every offspring survived, no trait would be favored.

questions.stem: In a forest, only a few seeds of each tree grow into adult trees. How does this fact contribute to natural selection?
options: It stops trees from making seeds
It lets all trees reproduce equally
questions.explanation: Organisms make more offspring than resources can support, so they compete. Those with helpful inherited traits survive and reproduce more, passing those traits on.

questions.stem: A river changes course and splits a population of mice into two groups. Over many generations, the groups can no longer interbreed. What process has occurred?
questions.explanation: Separation prevents gene flow, and each group changes as natural selection acts in its own environment. When they can no longer produce fertile offspring together, a new species has formed.

questions.stem: A storm kills most of a small population of lizards at random, and the survivors happen to have mostly one tail color. Which mechanism changed the population's gene pool?
questions.explanation: A random event that changes allele frequencies, especially in a small population, is genetic drift. Tail color did not affect who survived, so it was not selection.

questions.skill: B.13B Matter and energy through trophic levels
questions.stem: About how much energy is most likely stored in the hawks each year?
questions.explanation: Each level in this model holds about 10% of the level below it: 20,000, 2,000, 200. So the hawks hold about 10% of 200, or 20 kilocalories per square meter.

questions.skill: B.13B Matter and energy through trophic levels
questions.stem: What happens to most of the energy that is not passed from the grasshoppers to the mice?
options: It is stored in the soil forever
It is passed straight to the hawks
It is turned back into sunlight
questions.explanation: Organisms use most of the energy they take in for movement, growth and keeping warm, and it leaves as heat during respiration. Energy flows one way and is not recycled.

questions.skill: B.13B Matter and energy through trophic levels
questions.stem: A disease kills most of the grasshoppers. What is the most likely effect on the food chain?
options: Nothing else in the chain changes
questions.explanation: With fewer grasshoppers, less energy reaches the mice, so their numbers fall, and so do the hawks that eat them. The grasses would likely increase with fewer grazers.

questions.stem: Clownfish live among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones, which protect them from predators. The clownfish clean the anemone and drive away fish that eat it. This relationship is:
questions.explanation: Both species benefit, so the relationship is mutualism. In commensalism one benefits and the other is unaffected, and in parasitism one is harmed.

questions.stem: Bacteria in the roots of bean plants change nitrogen gas from the air into a form plants can use. Why is this important to ecosystems?
options: Plants need nitrogen gas to photosynthesize
Plants cannot use nitrogen gas directly
It makes carbon dioxide for plants
It removes all nitrogen from the soil
questions.explanation: Nitrogen gas makes up most of the air, but plants can absorb only fixed forms such as ammonium and nitrate. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria make nitrogen available to food webs.

questions.stem: A forest with many tree species is compared with a farm planted with one crop. A new plant disease arrives. Why is the forest more likely to stay stable?
options: One species does all the work there
It has fewer kinds of organisms
Its many species limit the spread
questions.explanation: When many species fill similar roles, losing one does not collapse the system, and a disease that attacks one species cannot spread to all. A field of one crop can be wiped out.

questions.stem: A protein's function depends most directly on its:
questions.explanation: The sequence of amino acids folds into a specific shape, and that shape lets a protein bind the molecules it acts on. Glucose units build carbohydrates and fatty acids build lipids.

questions.stem: Which biomolecule stores the instructions a cell uses to build its proteins?
questions.explanation: DNA is a nucleic acid whose sequence of bases codes for proteins. Glycogen and cellulose are carbohydrates, and cholesterol is a lipid found in membranes.

questions.stem: Which structure is found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
questions.explanation: Every cell makes proteins, so both cell types have ribosomes, though prokaryotic ribosomes are smaller. A nucleus, mitochondria and a Golgi apparatus are membrane-bound structures found only in eukaryotes.

questions.stem: HIV infects helper T cells, a type of white blood cell. Over time this makes a person more likely to develop other infections because:
options: red blood cells stop carrying oxygen
the virus turns T cells into bacteria
the virus attacks the skin directly
questions.explanation: Each new virus made inside a helper T cell destroys it, and helper T cells coordinate the immune response. As their number falls, the body cannot fight off infections it would normally control.

questions.skill: B.6A Cell cycle and DNA replication
questions.stem: During DNA replication, a parent strand that reads ATTGC is used as a template. Which sequence does the new strand have?
questions.explanation: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine, so ATTGC is matched by TAACG. Uracil is found in RNA, not DNA.

questions.stem: Some turtle eggs develop into males at cooler temperatures and females at warmer temperatures. This shows that:
questions.explanation: Temperature during development changes which genes are expressed, so the same genetic makeup can become either sex. The DNA sequence of the eggs is not changed.

questions.skill: B.6C Cell cycle disruptions and cancer
questions.stem: Which statement best describes cancer cells?
options: They contain no DNA at all
questions.explanation: Cancer cells have mutations that let them ignore the signals and checkpoints that normally regulate the cell cycle, so they divide again and again and can form tumors.

questions.stem: Which equation summarizes photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis uses light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. The reverse equation is cellular respiration, and the last one is fermentation.

questions.stem: Which two substances are products of cellular respiration? Choose two.
questions.explanation: Cellular respiration breaks down glucose using oxygen and releases carbon dioxide, water and energy stored in ATP. Glucose and oxygen are the reactants.

questions.stem: An enzyme from the human stomach works best at pH 2. If it is moved to a solution at pH 8, it will most likely:
questions.explanation: Each enzyme has a pH range where its shape fits its substrate best. Far from that range its shape changes and the reaction slows or stops.

questions.stem: When a person gets a cut, white blood cells travel to the wound in the blood. This shows the circulatory system working with the:
questions.explanation: The immune system defends against pathogens that enter through the wound, and the circulatory system carries its white blood cells there. Defense from injury and illness depends on both.

questions.stem: A plant's stem bends toward light coming from a window. Which statement best explains this response?
options: The leaves pull the stem toward the light
Water leaves the stem through the flowers
A hormone lengthens cells on the shaded side
Light pulls water into the stem's lit side
questions.explanation: Plant hormones called auxins collect on the shaded side of the stem and make those cells elongate, so the stem curves toward the light. This response is called phototropism.

questions.stem: Some flowers are brightly colored and make nectar. These structures help the plant reproduce mainly by:
questions.explanation: Pollinators such as bees visit flowers for nectar and carry pollen from one flower to another, which allows fertilization. Absorbing water is a job of the roots.

questions.stem: Which mutant version makes a protein identical to the normal protein?
questions.explanation: In Mutant 3, GAA became GAG, and both codons code for glutamic acid, so the protein is unchanged. Mutant 1 swaps glutamic acid for valine.

questions.skill: B.7B Gene expression and protein synthesis
questions.stem: How many amino acids are in the protein made from the normal gene?
questions.explanation: Methionine, glutamic acid, proline, phenylalanine and glycine make 5 amino acids. UAA is a stop codon, which ends translation without adding an amino acid.

questions.stem: Which change best describes Mutant 2?
options: A silent change in one codon
A deletion of a whole codon
A substitution of a single amino acid
questions.explanation: An extra U after the second codon shifts every codon after it, so every amino acid from that point is likely to change. A frameshift usually changes a protein more than a substitution does.

questions.stem: Some scientists propose that early life stored its genetic information in RNA before DNA. Which observation supports this idea?
options: RNA is found only in viruses
Some RNA can act as an enzyme
questions.explanation: Because some RNA molecules act as catalysts as well as carrying information, RNA could have done both jobs before DNA and proteins took them over. RNA is usually single stranded and contains uracil, not thymine.

questions.stem: During meiosis, homologous chromosomes exchange segments. How does this crossing-over affect a population?
options: It makes offspring identical to parents
questions.explanation: Crossing-over creates chromosomes with new combinations of alleles, so offspring differ from each other and from their parents. More variation in a population helps it survive change.

questions.stem: Blood type is controlled by three alleles, A, B and O, with A and B codominant and O recessive. A parent with type AB blood and a parent with type O blood can have children with which blood types?
questions.explanation: The AB parent passes A or B, and the OO parent passes O, so children are AO (type A) or BO (type B). No child can be AB or O.

questions.stem: Color blindness is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. A woman who carries the allele has children with a man who has normal vision. What fraction of their sons are expected to be color blind?
questions.explanation: Sons get their X chromosome from their mother, and a carrier mother passes the allele half the time. The father gives sons a Y, which does not carry the gene.

questions.stem: In pea plants, yellow seeds (Y) are dominant to green (y), and round seeds (R) are dominant to wrinkled (r). Two plants that are YyRr are crossed. What fraction of the offspring are expected to have green, wrinkled seeds?
questions.explanation: Green needs yy (1/4) and wrinkled needs rr (1/4). The genes sort independently, so 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16. Yellow, round is 9/16.

questions.stem: Australia has many marsupial species found nowhere else, even though other continents have similar habitats. This pattern is best explained by:
options: marsupials being unable to live elsewhere
all habitats producing the same species
questions.explanation: Biogeography, the study of where species live, shows that isolated regions develop their own groups of related species descended from shared ancestors in that region.

questions.stem: Early embryos of fish, chickens and humans all have similar structures, including pharyngeal pouches and a tail. This developmental homology suggests that these animals:
options: will develop the same adult form
eat the same kinds of food
questions.explanation: Shared patterns in early development are evidence that the species inherited the same developmental genes from a common ancestor. Their adult forms are very different.

questions.skill: B.9B Rates of change in the fossil record
questions.stem: A series of fossils shows a horse-like animal's leg bones changing slowly and steadily through many rock layers. This pattern supports the explanation of:
questions.explanation: Gradualism describes slow, continuous change over long periods, seen as small steps between layers. Stasis would show little change.

questions.skill: B.10A Natural selection acts on populations
questions.stem: What happened to the share of dark beetles in the population from year 0 to year 6?
options: It stayed near 50% the whole time
questions.explanation: Dark beetles were 50 of 500 at year 0 (10%) and 260 of 330 at year 6 (about 79%). The population changed, not individual beetles.

questions.stem: Which explanation best accounts for the change in beetle colors?
options: Dark beetles laid all the eggs
Light beetles turned dark to hide
Birds ate more of the light beetles
Dark soil caused mutations in the beetles
questions.explanation: On darkened soil, light beetles were easier for birds to see. Dark beetles survived and reproduced more, so the inherited dark color became more common.

questions.stem: Which part of the scenario shows that the population produces more offspring than can survive?
options: Birds eat beetles they can see easily
The soil changed color after a fire
More eggs are laid than survive
questions.explanation: Overproduction is the statement that more eggs are laid than survive to adulthood. Inheritance and predation are other parts of the explanation.

questions.stem: Dark beetles from a nearby burned area begin moving into this population and breeding with it. How will this most likely change the population?
options: The dark-color allele becomes more common
The light-color allele becomes more common
questions.explanation: The newcomers bring dark-color alleles with them. This movement of alleles with migrating individuals is gene flow, and here it adds to the change selection is already causing.

questions.stem: Two populations of frogs live in the same pond, but one mates in early spring and the other in late spring. Over time they become separate species. What kept them from interbreeding?
questions.explanation: Mating at different times is a reproductive barrier even without a physical barrier. With no gene flow, the populations can change separately until they become separate species.

questions.stem: Which relationship between wolves and elk is shown in the data?
questions.explanation: Wolves hunt and eat elk, so this is predation. As the wolf population grew, the elk population fell from 16,000 to 7,000.

questions.stem: Why did the number of young willows rise after wolves returned?
options: Elk began to protect the willows
Fewer elk ate the young trees
Willows grew better in cold years
questions.explanation: Elk eat young willows. With fewer elk grazing along streams, more young trees survived. A change at one trophic level affected the producers below it.

questions.stem: Willows shade streams and provide food for beavers. What is the most likely long-term effect of the willows' recovery?
options: Fewer species can live along the streams
More species can live along the streams
The wolves will start eating willows
questions.explanation: Restored plants provide food and habitat, so more kinds of organisms can live there. Higher biodiversity makes the ecosystem more stable.

questions.stem: Barnacles attach to the skin of a whale and are carried to places with food. The whale is neither helped nor harmed. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: One species benefits and the other is unaffected, which is commensalism. If the barnacles harmed the whale, it would be parasitism.

questions.stem: Burning large amounts of coal, oil and gas affects the carbon cycle mainly by:
options: adding carbon dioxide to the air
storing more carbon in the ground
removing carbon dioxide from the air
questions.explanation: Fossil fuels hold carbon stored over millions of years. Burning them releases it as carbon dioxide faster than photosynthesis and the oceans can take it up.

questions.skill: B.13B Matter and energy through trophic levels
questions.stem: Why are there usually far fewer top predators than producers in an ecosystem?
options: Energy increases up the food chain
questions.explanation: Only about a tenth of the energy at one level is passed to the next, so the top of a food chain has very little energy to support a population.

questions.stem: Which biomolecule do cells use as their main short-term source of energy?
questions.explanation: Sugars such as glucose are broken down quickly in cellular respiration to make ATP. Proteins can supply energy but are mainly used for structure and function, and nucleic acids carry information.

questions.stem: Enzymes, antibodies and the channels that move ions across membranes are all made of:
questions.explanation: Each of these jobs depends on a molecule with a precise shape, and proteins are the biomolecules folded into specific shapes from chains of amino acids.

questions.stem: Plant cell walls stay rigid largely because they contain:
questions.explanation: Cellulose is a carbohydrate made of long glucose chains that form strong fibers. Glycogen is the storage carbohydrate of animals and fungi, not a structural one.

questions.stem: A seal has a thick layer of fat under its skin. Besides storing energy, this lipid layer helps the seal:
questions.explanation: Fat is a poor conductor of heat, so it insulates the body as well as storing a large amount of energy. Hemoglobin, a protein, carries oxygen, and enzymes speed up reactions.

questions.stem: Heating an enzyme to a high temperature changes its shape but not its sequence of amino acids. Which level of structure was disrupted?
questions.explanation: Heat breaks the weak bonds that hold the chain in its folded shape, a change called denaturation. The peptide bonds linking amino acids stay intact, which is why the sequence is unchanged.

questions.stem: A cell with a nucleus, mitochondria and an endoplasmic reticulum is a:
questions.explanation: Membrane-bound organelles such as the nucleus and mitochondria are found only in eukaryotic cells. Bacteria are prokaryotes, and a virus is not a cell.

questions.stem: In a prokaryotic cell, where is most of the DNA found?
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes have no nucleus, so their circular chromosome sits in a region of the cytoplasm called the nucleoid. A nucleus surrounded by a membrane is a eukaryotic feature.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
questions.explanation: Eukaryotic cells are typically about 10 times larger across and divide their work among membrane-bound organelles. Both cell types have DNA and a cell membrane.

questions.stem: Chloroplasts have two membranes, their own DNA and ribosomes like those of bacteria. These facts are best explained by the idea that chloroplasts:
options: are viruses living inside plant cells
were made by the cell's nucleus
formed from folds of the cell membrane
questions.explanation: Endosymbiotic theory explains a double membrane, separate DNA and bacteria-like ribosomes as signs that an ancestral cell took in a photosynthetic prokaryote. The infolding explanation accounts for organelles such as the endoplasmic reticulum, which have no DNA of their own.

questions.stem: Which structure would you find in a plant cell but not in a bacterium?
questions.explanation: Bacteria also have a cell wall, ribosomes and a cell membrane. Chloroplasts are membrane-bound organelles, so only eukaryotes such as plants and algae have them.

questions.stem: A eukaryotic cell can carry out many different reactions at the same time without them interfering. This is mainly because:
options: its DNA floats freely in the cell
it makes no proteins at all
questions.explanation: Organelles surrounded by membranes keep different conditions and enzymes in separate spaces, such as digestive enzymes inside lysosomes. This compartmentalization is one reason eukaryotic cells can be large and complex.

questions.stem: A virus is made of genetic material surrounded by:
questions.explanation: A virus particle has DNA or RNA inside a protein coat called a capsid, and some also have an outer envelope. It has no cytoplasm, nucleus or cell wall.

questions.stem: Why are viruses not considered living cells?
options: They copy only inside a host cell
They are larger than most bacteria
questions.explanation: A virus has no ribosomes or metabolism of its own, so it can only be copied by taking over a host cell. Viruses do carry DNA or RNA, and most are far smaller than bacteria.

questions.stem: A flu virus attaches only to cells lining the airways. What explains why it infects those cells and not others?
options: It is too large to enter other cells
questions.explanation: A virus enters a cell when its surface proteins bind specific receptor molecules on the host cell. Cells without the matching receptors are not infected.

questions.stem: Washing hands often during flu season reduces the spread of the virus mainly because it:
options: removes virus particles from the skin
changes the virus into a harmless cell
makes the body produce more antibiotics
kills the bacteria that carry the virus
questions.explanation: Many viruses spread when hands pick up particles from surfaces or coughs and then touch the face. Washing removes those particles. Viruses are not carried by bacteria, and the body does not make antibiotics.

questions.stem: Which two features do viruses and cells share? Choose two.
questions.explanation: Viruses have DNA or RNA and a protein coat, so they share genetic material and proteins with cells. They make no ATP, have no ribosomes and are copied inside a host, not divided by mitosis.

questions.skill: B.6A Cell cycle and DNA replication
questions.stem: What is the main role of mitosis in a multicellular organism?
options: Growth and repair of the body
questions.explanation: Mitosis produces two daughter cells with the same chromosomes as the parent, which lets an organism grow and replace damaged cells. Gametes are made by meiosis.

questions.skill: B.6A Cell cycle and DNA replication
questions.stem: In which phase of mitosis do the sister chromatids separate and move to opposite ends of the cell?
questions.explanation: In anaphase the sister chromatids are pulled apart toward opposite poles. In metaphase they line up across the middle of the cell, and in telophase new nuclei form.

questions.skill: B.6A Cell cycle and DNA replication
questions.stem: A cell with 46 chromosomes completes mitosis. How many chromosomes does each daughter cell have?
questions.explanation: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same, so each daughter cell gets 46. Halving to 23 happens in meiosis.

questions.skill: B.6A Cell cycle and DNA replication
questions.stem: The longest part of the cell cycle for most cells, when the cell grows and carries out its normal work, is:
questions.explanation: A cell spends most of its life in interphase, which includes growth and the copying of DNA. Mitosis and cytokinesis are short by comparison.

questions.skill: B.6A Cell cycle and DNA replication
questions.stem: Before replication, a DNA molecule is labeled so both strands are heavy. It then copies once in a medium with only light nucleotides. If replication is semiconservative, each new molecule will be:
questions.explanation: Each new molecule keeps one heavy parent strand and builds one light strand, so every molecule is a hybrid. A fully heavy molecule would only appear under the conservative model.

questions.skill: B.6A Cell cycle and DNA replication
questions.stem: Why must a cell copy its DNA before it divides by mitosis?
options: So the new cells have half the DNA
So each new cell gets all the genes
So the cell can make more mitochondria
So the DNA can change its sequence
questions.explanation: Replication makes two identical copies of each chromosome, and mitosis gives one copy to each daughter cell, so both have complete genetic information.

questions.stem: The process by which an unspecialized cell becomes a specific type of cell, such as a muscle cell, is called:
questions.explanation: Differentiation is the change from a general cell to a specialized one with a particular structure and job. Replication is the copying of DNA.

questions.stem: Why are stem cells useful to scientists studying how to repair damaged tissue?
options: They can become many cell types
They have more DNA than other cells
questions.explanation: Stem cells are unspecialized and can differentiate into different kinds of cells, so they could replace cells lost to injury or disease.

questions.stem: Hydrangea plants with the same genes grow blue flowers in acidic soil and pink flowers in less acidic soil. The difference is caused by:
questions.explanation: The plants share their genes, so the color difference comes from soil conditions that affect how flower cells develop and which pigments they show.

questions.stem: In a developing embryo, cells on one side receive a chemical signal that cells on the other side do not. The signal most likely causes the cells that receive it to:
options: turn on a different set of genes
become identical to the other cells
questions.explanation: Signals from neighboring cells are one of the environmental factors that direct differentiation by turning certain genes on or off. They do not remove chromosomes.

questions.skill: B.6C Cell cycle disruptions and cancer
questions.stem: A mass of cells that forms when cells divide uncontrollably is called a:
questions.explanation: Uncontrolled division makes an abnormal mass called a tumor, which may be benign or cancerous. Tissues and organs form from normal, regulated division and differentiation.

questions.skill: B.6C Cell cycle disruptions and cancer
questions.stem: Which factor increases the risk of cancer by damaging DNA in skin cells?
questions.explanation: UV radiation can damage DNA. If the damage hits genes that control the cell cycle and is not repaired, cells may begin dividing without control.

questions.skill: B.6C Cell cycle disruptions and cancer
questions.stem: Many cancer drugs work by stopping cells from completing mitosis. Why do these drugs also cause side effects such as hair loss?
options: The drugs change hair cells' genes
Hair is made by cancer cells
questions.explanation: These drugs target any rapidly dividing cell, and cells in hair follicles divide often. The drugs cannot tell those normal dividing cells from cancer cells.

questions.skill: B.6C Cell cycle disruptions and cancer
questions.stem: Which two changes could lead to uncontrolled cell division? Choose two.
options: A checkpoint protein that stops working
A growth signal that stays switched on
A cell that dies after DNA damage
A cell that pauses to repair its DNA
A cell that stops at its normal size
questions.explanation: Cancer can result when signals that tell a cell to divide are always active or when the checks that stop division are lost. Pausing to repair, cell death after damage and stopping at a normal size are all normal controls.

questions.stem: In which organelle does photosynthesis take place?
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy for photosynthesis. Mitochondria are where most of cellular respiration happens.

questions.stem: Most of the ATP made in cellular respiration is produced in the:
questions.explanation: The later stages of aerobic respiration take place in the mitochondria and produce most of the ATP. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis.

questions.stem: The energy stored in glucose made by a plant originally came from:
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy held in the bonds of glucose. Water and carbon dioxide supply the atoms, not the energy.

questions.stem: The oxygen gas that plants release during photosynthesis comes from:
questions.explanation: During the light-dependent reactions, water is split, and its oxygen is released as oxygen gas. The carbon dioxide is used to build glucose.

questions.stem: Why do plant cells need mitochondria even though they have chloroplasts?
options: To make glucose from carbon dioxide
To store water for the cell
To release energy from glucose as ATP
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts make glucose, but plant cells, like animal cells, must break glucose down in cellular respiration to make the ATP that powers their work.

questions.stem: A plant takes in 6 molecules of carbon dioxide and 6 of water to make glucose. How many carbon atoms are in the glucose made?
questions.explanation: Matter is conserved: the 6 carbon atoms from 6 CO2 end up in one glucose molecule, C6H12O6.

questions.stem: A sealed jar holds a plant in the dark. Over a day, the carbon dioxide level in the jar rises. This happens because the plant:
options: carries out respiration but not photosynthesis
carries out photosynthesis but not respiration
questions.explanation: Without light the plant cannot photosynthesize, but it keeps respiring, which releases carbon dioxide. In light, photosynthesis would use carbon dioxide faster than respiration releases it.

questions.stem: How are photosynthesis and cellular respiration related?
options: Both release oxygen into the air
Both take place only in animals
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis makes glucose and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water, and respiration uses glucose and oxygen to make carbon dioxide and water. Matter cycles between the two processes.

questions.stem: Enzymes are biomolecules that:
questions.explanation: Enzymes are proteins that act as catalysts, speeding up reactions in cells. DNA stores information and lipids form membranes.

questions.stem: The part of an enzyme where the substrate binds is called the:
questions.explanation: The substrate fits into the active site, a pocket with a specific shape. A change to that shape stops the substrate from binding.

questions.stem: Lactase breaks down the sugar lactose but has no effect on starch. The best explanation is that:
options: only lactose fits its active site
starch molecules are too small to bind
lactase is used up by lactose
questions.explanation: An enzyme is specific because its active site fits the shape of one substrate. Starch is a carbohydrate, but its shape does not match lactase's active site.

questions.stem: After an enzyme helps one reaction, what happens to the enzyme?
questions.explanation: Catalysts are not consumed, so the enzyme releases the products unchanged and can bind another substrate molecule.

questions.stem: A student adds more and more substrate to a fixed amount of enzyme. The reaction rate rises, then levels off. Why does it level off?
options: The enzyme has been used up
All the active sites are in use
questions.explanation: Once every enzyme molecule is working, adding more substrate cannot speed the reaction. The enzyme is not used up; it is simply saturated.

questions.stem: Without enzymes, most reactions in cells would:
options: be far too slow for life
questions.explanation: Many cell reactions have a high activation energy and would take far too long at body temperature without enzymes lowering that barrier.

questions.stem: Which two conditions can change the shape of an enzyme and slow its reaction? Choose two.
options: Keeping it at its best temperature
A pH far from its best level
questions.explanation: Extreme temperature and pH disrupt the bonds that hold an enzyme's shape, which changes the active site. More substrate or reuse does not change the enzyme.

questions.stem: Oxygen enters the blood in the lungs and is carried to body cells. Which two systems are involved?
questions.explanation: The respiratory system takes in oxygen at the lungs, and the circulatory system moves oxygen-rich blood to cells throughout the body.

questions.stem: When you touch a hot pan, you pull your hand away before you feel pain. Which systems work together in this response?
questions.explanation: Sensory nerves send a signal to the spinal cord, which signals muscles in the arm to contract and pull the hand away. This is a reflex.

questions.stem: On a hot day, a person sweats and blood vessels near the skin widen. These responses help the body:
options: fight off bacteria in the skin
questions.explanation: Sweating cools the skin as water evaporates, and wider vessels near the skin release heat. Both are regulation that keeps the internal temperature stable.

questions.stem: The hormone FSH from the pituitary gland causes eggs to mature in the ovaries. This is an example of the endocrine system working with the:
questions.explanation: Hormones from the pituitary gland regulate the reproductive organs, so reproduction depends on both systems.

questions.stem: Villi are tiny folds lining the small intestine, each with many blood vessels. How do villi help the body?
options: They push food back to the stomach
They add surface area for absorption
They make digestive enzymes for the liver
They store water for the kidneys
questions.explanation: Villi greatly increase the surface area of the intestine wall, and the nearby blood vessels carry the absorbed nutrients away quickly.

questions.stem: Which body system first blocks most pathogens from entering the body?
questions.explanation: Unbroken skin, part of the integumentary system, is a physical barrier that keeps most pathogens out. The immune system responds when pathogens get past it.

questions.stem: A vaccine contains a weakened or inactive form of a virus. It protects a person because it:
options: prepares the immune system to respond
kills bacteria already in the body
replaces the person's white blood cells
stops the heart from pumping the virus
questions.explanation: The immune system makes antibodies and memory cells against the vaccine, so it can respond quickly if the real virus enters later.

questions.stem: The kidneys filter wastes from the blood. Which system brings that blood to the kidneys?
questions.explanation: The circulatory system carries blood through the kidneys, where the excretory system removes wastes and makes urine.

questions.stem: Sugars made in the leaves are carried to the roots through:
questions.explanation: Phloem transports sugars from where they are made to where they are used or stored. Xylem carries water up from the roots.

questions.stem: Stomata are small openings on leaves. Guard cells close the stomata on a hot, dry day. This helps the plant:
questions.explanation: Closing the stomata reduces water loss by evaporation. The trade-off is that less carbon dioxide can enter for photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Root hairs are thin extensions of root cells. Their main function is to:
questions.explanation: Root hairs add a large amount of surface area, so the roots can absorb more water and minerals from the soil.

questions.stem: A seedling's roots grow downward even when the seed is planted upside down. This response to gravity is called:
questions.explanation: Gravitropism is growth in response to gravity: roots grow down and shoots grow up. Phototropism is growth toward light.

questions.stem: Water evaporating from leaves pulls more water up through the xylem from the roots. Which pair of plant systems does this connect?
questions.explanation: Transpiration from the leaves of the shoot system creates a pull that draws water absorbed by the root system up the xylem.

questions.stem: After pollination, the ovary of a flower develops into a fruit. How does a fruit help a plant reproduce?
options: It carries water to the roots
It makes pollen for other flowers
It absorbs sunlight for the seeds
questions.explanation: Animals eat fruits and drop or pass the seeds away from the parent plant, and some fruits are carried by wind or water. Spreading seeds reduces crowding and competition.

questions.stem: Which two structures does a flowering plant use for sexual reproduction? Choose two.
questions.explanation: Stamens make pollen and pistils hold the ovules, so both take part in fertilization. Root hairs absorb water, guard cells control the stomata and xylem carries water.

questions.stem: Which base pairs with guanine in a DNA molecule?
questions.explanation: Guanine always pairs with cytosine, and adenine pairs with thymine. Uracil is found in RNA, not DNA.

questions.stem: The order of bases in a gene determines a trait mainly by determining the:
options: number of chromosomes in a cell
amino acid order in a protein
amount of sugar in the DNA
questions.explanation: Each set of three bases codes for an amino acid, so the base sequence sets the amino acid sequence, which shapes the protein that produces the trait.

questions.stem: The two strands of a DNA double helix are held together by bonds between:
questions.explanation: Weak hydrogen bonds between complementary bases join the two strands. The sugar and phosphate groups form the backbone of each strand.

questions.stem: A sample of DNA is 30% adenine. What percent of the sample is thymine?
questions.explanation: Adenine pairs with thymine, so they are present in equal amounts: 30% thymine. That leaves 40% for guanine and cytosine together, 20% each.

questions.skill: B.7B Gene expression and protein synthesis
questions.stem: Where in a eukaryotic cell does translation take place?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes in the cytoplasm and on the endoplasmic reticulum read mRNA and join amino acids into proteins. Transcription happens in the nucleus.

questions.skill: B.7B Gene expression and protein synthesis
questions.stem: A DNA template strand reads TAC GGA. What mRNA is transcribed from it?
questions.explanation: RNA pairs with the template: T pairs with A, A with U, C with G and G with C, giving AUG CCU. RNA uses U in place of T.

questions.skill: B.7B Gene expression and protein synthesis
questions.stem: What is the job of transfer RNA during protein synthesis?
options: It brings amino acids to the ribosome
It carries the protein out of the cell
It joins the two DNA strands
It copies the gene in the nucleus
questions.explanation: Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon that pairs with a codon on the mRNA, placing amino acids in the right order.

questions.skill: B.7B Gene expression and protein synthesis
questions.stem: An mRNA molecule has 300 bases from its start codon to just before its stop codon. How many amino acids does it code for?
questions.explanation: A codon is three bases, so 300 bases are 100 codons, each adding one amino acid.

questions.skill: B.7B Gene expression and protein synthesis
questions.stem: Pancreas cells make large amounts of insulin, but skin cells make none, even though both have the insulin gene. This is because:
options: insulin is made from fat, not protein
skin cells have a mutated insulin gene
only some cells express the gene
questions.explanation: Gene expression is controlled, so a gene is transcribed and translated only in cells that need its protein. The gene is present in both cell types.

questions.stem: A permanent change in the sequence of DNA is called a:
questions.explanation: A mutation is any change in the DNA base sequence. A codon is a group of three bases, and a nucleotide is one unit of DNA.

questions.stem: In sickle cell disease, one base change in the hemoglobin gene replaces one amino acid. Which kind of mutation is this?
questions.explanation: Replacing one base with another is a substitution. Here it changes one amino acid, which alters the shape of hemoglobin and of red blood cells.

questions.stem: Why does deleting one base near the start of a gene usually harm the protein more than deleting one base near the end?
options: It adds a new start codon
It changes only the stop codon
questions.explanation: A single-base deletion is a frameshift, so every codon after it is read wrongly. Near the start, almost the whole protein is changed.

questions.stem: A mutation occurs in a skin cell on a person's arm. Can the mutation be passed on to the person's children?
options: No, because it is not in a sex cell
Yes, because all cells make gametes
No, because skin cells have no DNA
Yes, because skin cells become eggs
questions.explanation: Only mutations in cells that make eggs or sperm can be inherited. A mutation in a body cell affects that cell and the cells it divides into.

questions.stem: Which two changes are frameshift mutations? Choose two.
questions.explanation: Adding or removing a number of bases that is not a multiple of three shifts the reading frame. Deleting three bases removes one codon and keeps the frame, and a replacement keeps it too.

questions.stem: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in a human egg cell?
questions.explanation: Meiosis reduces the chromosome number by half, so eggs and sperm have 23. Fertilization joins two gametes to restore 46.

questions.stem: Why is it important that gametes have half the number of chromosomes of body cells?
options: So the zygote has the normal number
So the parent loses no genes
So the gamete can divide by mitosis
questions.explanation: When an egg and sperm join, their chromosomes combine. If each had a full set, the number would double every generation.

questions.stem: Independent assortment during meiosis means that:
options: every gamete gets the same chromosomes
DNA is copied twice before meiosis
questions.explanation: Each pair of homologous chromosomes lines up independently of the others, so gametes get many different mixes of maternal and paternal chromosomes.

questions.stem: An organism has 3 pairs of chromosomes. Counting independent assortment alone, how many different combinations of chromosomes can its gametes have?
questions.explanation: Each pair can go two ways, so 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 combinations. Crossing-over adds even more variety.

questions.stem: Which outcome of sexual reproduction is a direct result of meiosis and fertilization?
options: Offspring that are clones of one parent
Offspring that differ from their parents
Offspring with twice the parents' chromosomes
questions.explanation: Meiosis shuffles alleles and fertilization combines them from two parents, so each offspring has a new combination. Clones come from asexual reproduction.

questions.stem: An organism with two different alleles for a gene, such as Tt, is called:
questions.explanation: Heterozygous means the two alleles differ. TT or tt would be homozygous.

questions.stem: In guinea pigs, black fur (B) is dominant to white fur (b). Two heterozygous black guinea pigs are crossed. What fraction of their offspring are expected to have white fur?
questions.explanation: Bb x Bb gives BB, Bb, Bb and bb, so 1/4 are bb and white.

questions.stem: A tall plant (T, dominant) is crossed with a short plant (tt). All 40 offspring are tall. What is the most likely genotype of the tall parent?
questions.explanation: If the tall parent were Tt, about half the offspring would be short. Getting no short offspring among 40 points to TT.

questions.stem: In some cattle, a red bull crossed with a white cow gives a calf with both red and white hairs. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Both alleles are fully expressed, as separate red and white hairs, so this is codominance. Incomplete dominance would give one blended color.

questions.stem: Hemophilia is an X-linked recessive disorder. Why is it more common in males than in females?
options: The allele is on the Y chromosome
Males have only one X chromosome
questions.explanation: A male with one recessive allele on his only X shows the disorder. A female needs the allele on both X chromosomes.

questions.stem: A person with type A blood and a person with type B blood have a child with type O blood. What are the parents' genotypes?
questions.explanation: A type O child is OO, so each parent must carry an O allele. A type A parent with O is AO and a type B parent with O is BO.

questions.stem: Two plants that are both heterozygous for two genes on different chromosomes are crossed. What phenotype ratio is expected?
questions.explanation: A dihybrid cross of two heterozygotes gives 9 with both dominant traits, 3 and 3 with one of each, and 1 with both recessive traits.

questions.stem: Which two crosses can produce offspring with a recessive phenotype? Choose two.
questions.explanation: A recessive phenotype needs aa, so both parents must carry at least one a. AA x aa gives only Aa, and the crosses with an AA parent always give at least one A.

questions.stem: Fossils found in lower rock layers are generally:
options: younger than those in higher layers
the same age as those above
older than those in higher layers
questions.explanation: Sedimentary rock forms in layers, with newer layers laid on top, so in undisturbed rock the deeper fossils are older.

questions.stem: Whales have small hip bones that are not connected to the backbone and are not used for walking. Scientists use such structures as evidence that whales:
options: use the bones to swim faster
will grow legs in the future
questions.explanation: Reduced structures with little or no function are vestigial structures. Whale hip bones match the hip bones of land mammals, pointing to shared ancestry.

questions.stem: Humans and chimpanzees share about 98% of their DNA sequence. This is an example of which kind of evidence?
questions.explanation: Similar DNA and protein sequences are molecular evidence of common ancestry. The more similar the sequences, the more closely related the species.

questions.stem: Bird wings and butterfly wings both help the animals fly, but they are built very differently. These wings are:
questions.explanation: Analogous structures do a similar job but come from different ancestral structures, so they are not evidence of close common ancestry.

questions.stem: Islands near a continent often have species that are similar to, but different from, species on the nearby mainland. This pattern suggests that:
options: island species were never related to mainland ones
mainland species descended from island ones only
island species descended from mainland ancestors
questions.explanation: Biogeography shows that organisms that reached the islands from the mainland changed over time in their new environment, so island species resemble their mainland relatives.

questions.stem: A fossil has features of both fish and four-legged land animals, including fins with wrist-like bones. Fossils like this are called:
questions.explanation: Transitional fossils show a mix of features of an ancestral group and a descendant group, filling in steps of the fossil record.

questions.stem: Four species are compared using the number of differences in one protein from species W: X has 2, Y has 9 and Z has 15. Which species is most closely related to W?
questions.explanation: The fewest differences, 2, means species X shares the most recent common ancestor with W.

questions.stem: Many very different organisms use the same genetic code to make proteins. This is evidence that:
questions.explanation: The same codons stand for the same amino acids in bacteria, plants and animals, which is best explained by inheritance from a shared ancestor.

questions.skill: B.9B Rates of change in the fossil record
questions.stem: Little or no change in a species over a long period of the fossil record is called:
questions.explanation: Stasis describes long stretches when a species' form stays nearly the same in the fossil record.

questions.skill: B.9B Rates of change in the fossil record
questions.stem: Two scientists disagree about whether a group of fossil snails changed gradually or appeared abruptly. Which new evidence would best help them decide?
options: Fossils from only the top rock layer
Fossils from many closely spaced rock layers
The color of a single shell
questions.explanation: Telling a slow, steady change from a sudden one needs a detailed sequence through time. Many closely spaced layers show whether in-between forms are present.

questions.skill: B.9B Rates of change in the fossil record
questions.stem: Many new animal groups appear in rock layers formed over a geologically short time in the Cambrian period. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: The sudden showing of many new forms in a short span of the record is called abrupt appearance. Scientists examine several explanations for it, including fast change and gaps in preservation.

questions.skill: B.9B Rates of change in the fossil record
questions.stem: Why might the fossil record show a group appearing abruptly even if its change was not sudden?
options: Rock layers never form on land
questions.explanation: Fossils form only under special conditions, so many steps may never be preserved. Gaps in preservation are one explanation scientists examine for abrupt appearance.

questions.skill: B.9B Rates of change in the fossil record
questions.stem: A species of crab has looked almost the same for millions of years. Which explanation could account for this stasis?
options: It reproduced much faster than others
Its DNA cannot mutate at all
questions.explanation: When conditions stay much the same, the traits that already work well keep being favored, so little change builds up. All species' DNA can mutate.

questions.stem: Which two observations are anatomical evidence of common ancestry? Choose two.
options: Similar DNA sequences in two species
Similar bone patterns in different limbs
Fossils found in the same rock layer
Reduced structures that resemble working ones
questions.explanation: Homologous and vestigial structures are both anatomical evidence. DNA sequences are molecular evidence, island species are biogeography and rock layers are the fossil record.

questions.skill: B.10A Natural selection acts on populations
questions.stem: Natural selection produces evolutionary change in:
options: a single cell in a day
questions.explanation: Individuals do not evolve. Over generations, inherited traits that help survival and reproduction become more common in the population.

questions.skill: B.10A Natural selection acts on populations
questions.stem: When an antibiotic is used, a few bacteria survive because they already carry a resistance gene. Later, most of the population is resistant. This happened because:
options: each bacterium chose to change its genes
the antibiotic created the resistance gene
the antibiotic taught bacteria to resist
questions.explanation: The resistance gene was already present. The antibiotic killed susceptible bacteria, so the resistant ones left more offspring and the population changed.

questions.skill: B.10A Natural selection acts on populations
questions.stem: In one region, light-colored mice are most common on pale sand, and dark-colored mice are most common on nearby dark lava rock. Owls hunt in both places. What does this pattern show about natural selection?
options: Mice change their fur color to match the ground
Owls cause new fur colors to appear
Which trait is favored depends on the environment
Dark fur is always better than light fur
questions.explanation: Owls catch the mice that stand out most, so the favored color differs between habitats. Fur color is inherited; the mice do not change color, and the owls do not create new alleles.

questions.skill: B.10A Natural selection acts on populations
questions.stem: Moths in a city were mostly light. After factories coated trees with soot, dark moths became more common over many generations. What changed in the moth population?
options: How common the dark allele is
Each moth's color during its life
questions.explanation: Selection by birds favored dark moths on dark trees, so the dark allele became more frequent in the population. Individual moths kept their colors.

questions.stem: In natural selection, organisms best suited to their environment tend to:
questions.explanation: Individuals with helpful inherited traits survive and leave more offspring, which is called differential reproductive success.

questions.stem: A finite supply of food in an environment leads to:
questions.explanation: Because resources are limited, not every individual can survive, so organisms compete. This is one element of natural selection.

questions.stem: During a drought, only finches with large, deep beaks can crack the hard seeds left. What is the most likely result in the next generation?
options: Every finch with a small beak
questions.explanation: Large-beaked finches survive and reproduce more, and beak size is inherited, so the next generation's average beak depth rises.

questions.stem: Where does the inherited variation that natural selection acts on come from?
options: Changes made during an organism's life
questions.explanation: New alleles come from mutations, and meiosis and fertilization create new combinations. Selection sorts that variation but does not create it.

questions.stem: A new species has formed when two populations:
questions.explanation: The usual test is reproductive isolation: members of the two groups cannot interbreed and produce fertile offspring.

questions.stem: Squirrels on the north and south rims of a deep canyon have been separated for a very long time and look different. What first led to their differences?
questions.explanation: A geographic barrier keeps the populations apart, so mutations, selection and drift change each group separately over time.

questions.stem: On an island chain, one ancestral bird species gave rise to many species with different beaks suited to different foods. This is best explained by:
options: every bird having the same beak
a single random mutation in one bird
questions.explanation: Groups that reached different islands faced different food sources, so different beak shapes were favored. Over time the isolated groups became separate species.

questions.stem: The movement of alleles between populations when individuals migrate is called:
questions.explanation: Gene flow moves alleles from one population to another and tends to make the populations more alike.

questions.stem: Genetic drift has a larger effect on:
questions.explanation: Random chance changes allele frequencies more in small populations, where a few individuals make up a large share of the gene pool.

questions.stem: A few birds fly to a new island and start a population. The new population has different allele frequencies from the mainland just by chance. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: When a small group starts a new population, its alleles may not match the original population by chance. This founder effect is a kind of genetic drift.

questions.stem: Which two mechanisms can change a gene pool without natural selection? Choose two.
questions.explanation: Drift and gene flow change allele frequencies through chance and migration. Variation, overproduction and limited resources are the elements of natural selection itself.

questions.stem: A tick feeds on the blood of a deer and can spread disease to it. This relationship is:
questions.explanation: The tick benefits and the deer is harmed but not usually killed, which is parasitism. A predator kills and eats its prey.

questions.stem: Two species of birds eat the same kind of seeds in a meadow where seeds are limited. This interaction is:
questions.explanation: When two species need the same limited resource, they compete, and each has less to use.

questions.stem: Bees collect nectar from flowers and carry pollen between them. How does this relationship affect the ecosystem?
options: It reduces the number of seeds
It removes nectar from the food web
questions.explanation: This mutualism feeds the bees and pollinates the plants, which make seeds and fruit that other organisms eat. Losing pollinators would hurt many species.

questions.stem: Sea otters eat sea urchins, which eat kelp. If the sea otters are removed, what is the most likely result?
options: Nothing changes in the kelp forest
questions.explanation: Without the predator, the urchin population grows and overgrazes the kelp, which many other species depend on. A predator can help keep an ecosystem stable.

questions.skill: B.13B Matter and energy through trophic levels
questions.stem: Organisms that make their own food from sunlight are called:
questions.explanation: Producers such as plants and algae capture light energy in photosynthesis and form the base of food chains.

questions.skill: B.13B Matter and energy through trophic levels
questions.stem: What is the role of decomposers such as fungi and bacteria in an ecosystem?
questions.explanation: Decomposers break down dead organisms and wastes, releasing matter such as nitrogen and carbon back into the soil and air for producers to use.

questions.skill: B.13B Matter and energy through trophic levels
questions.stem: A pond's producers store 50,000 units of energy. About how much energy can reach the secondary consumers?
questions.explanation: About 10% passes to each level: 5,000 reach the primary consumers and about 500 reach the secondary consumers.

questions.skill: B.13B Matter and energy through trophic levels
questions.stem: In an energy pyramid, why is the producer level the widest?
questions.explanation: Producers capture energy from the sun, and every level above gets a smaller share, so the base holds the most.

questions.stem: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Plants and algae take in carbon dioxide and build it into sugars. Respiration, burning and decomposition all release carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Fertilizer from farms washes into a lake and causes algae to grow very quickly. When the algae die and decompose, fish die. Why?
options: Algae release poison into all lakes
The fertilizer turns into carbon dioxide gas
Decomposers use up the oxygen in the water
Fish eat too much of the algae
questions.explanation: Extra nitrogen and phosphorus feed an algal bloom, and bacteria decomposing the dead algae use up dissolved oxygen, so fish suffocate. This disrupts the nitrogen cycle.

questions.stem: Where is carbon stored in a forest ecosystem?
questions.explanation: Carbon is part of every organic molecule, so trees, animals and soil organisms store large amounts. It also cycles through the air and oceans.

questions.stem: A large area of forest is cut down and burned. How does this affect the carbon cycle?
options: More carbon dioxide enters the air
Less carbon dioxide enters the air
questions.explanation: Burning releases the carbon stored in the trees, and fewer trees remain to take carbon dioxide back out of the air by photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Which human activity most directly reduces biodiversity in an area?
questions.explanation: Habitat loss is a leading cause of lost species, because organisms lose the food and shelter they need. The other actions help biodiversity.

questions.stem: An invasive plant spreads quickly in a wetland and crowds out native plants. What is the likely effect on the wetland's biodiversity?
questions.explanation: With no natural enemies, an invasive species can take over resources, so native species and the animals that depend on them decline.

questions.stem: Rising ocean temperatures cause many corals to die. Coral reefs shelter thousands of species. What is the most likely result?
questions.explanation: Corals build the habitat that reef fish and invertebrates need, so losing them lowers biodiversity and makes the whole ecosystem less stable.

questions.stem: Which two actions help keep an ecosystem's biodiversity high? Choose two.
questions.explanation: Protecting habitat and removing invaders let native species survive. Draining wetlands, clearing forests and fertilizer runoff all reduce biodiversity.
